claims_disputed.claim: Verbose responses and many information-providing turns lower satisfaction; proactive interaction raises it.
claims_disputed.reason: Beyond small n, the p-values in Table 7 come from backward elimination (18 of 21 predictors removed, §4.2) on 32 dialogues after ad-hoc removal of two outliers; post-selection p-values are not valid inference, and the relation is purely correlational. 'Weak' overstates what a stepwise fit on 32 points can show.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: The rubber-stamping evidence is from Prolific crowd-workers without HIPAA expertise (§3.4, §7), who were not acting as accountable approvers. It shows non-expert review is weak, not that an expert approval gate fails; the evidence does not generalize to the gate as a pattern.

missed_issues: Participant accounting: 49 = 8 pilot + 41 main; 49 − 15 removed = 34 dialogues, which implies pilot participants (4 of them students from the authors' university) are included in the analysed data (§3.4, Table 3); 41 − 15 would be 26.
Chance baseline of 0.25 for satisfaction-level F1 assumes uniform four-class labels; no majority-class or label-distribution baseline is given, so 'modestly above chance' is not established.
Agent outputs were 'manually extracted' from dialogues by the authors and compared to a ground truth also made by the authors' experts (§3.1, §4.1.1); no blinding.
Post-selection inference: stepwise backward elimination invalidates the reported p-values.
Relevance overstated: the team does healthcare education content ingestion/delivery, not EHR HIPAA compliance; the paper studies chat dialogue satisfaction, not a harness component.
note: The review is accurate on facts and its code-location F1 inconsistency check is correct (mean per-item F1 cannot exceed (0.151+0.142)/2). I disagree on relevance (4→2), generalizability (one academic codebase, one model → 1), and on reading crowd-worker agreement as evidence against expert approval gates.
